tier_reason: gpu_fft.txt (release 3.0, 2015, by the library author) gives a per-transform table with GPU_FFT at batch 1 and 10 next to FFTW_MEASURE on a Pi 1 with L2 cache enabled; every number in the record matches, and the ratios are correctly marked as derived. The harness hello_fft.c times only the GPU side and its makefile runs plain gcc with no optimization flag; the FFTW harness, FFTW version and FFTW build flags are not published, so this is first-party and partly reproducible: tier C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: GPU side: hello_fft makefile runs 'gcc -o hello_fft.bin <sources> -lrt -lm -ldl' with no -O flag; the transform runs in hand-written VideoCore IV QPU assembly (qasm/*.qasm assembled to hex/*.hex), so host flags matter little. FFTW side: version, compiler and flags not stated.
corrections.caveats: First-party table from the library's own doc file (gpu_fft.txt, release 3.0, Andrew Holme, 2015), measured on a 700 MHz Pi 1 with VC4 L2 cache enabled. The baseline is FFTW_MEASURE on the same Pi 1 ARM11 CPU; FFTW version, build flags and the FFTW timing code are not published (hello_fft.c times only GPU_FFT). The doc says FFTW is still one order of magnitude more accurate (GPU_FFT rms error 0.33-1.5 ppm, single precision, output not scaled). Kernels are VideoCore IV QPU assembly, so they target the BCM2835-family GPU (Pi 1-3/Zero; gpu_fft_base.c has a Pi 2 memory path) and need root plus the mailbox device; they do not carry over to other GPUs. The repo was archived on 2025-08-27 and its README calls it 'ancient and deprecated'. Last commit date is for the hello_fft directory. The author's GPU_FFT web page was not opened.

notes: Judged only the hello_fft component. QPU assembly sources (qasm/) and C files carry Andrew Holme's BSD-3-Clause header; repo LICENCE is also BSD-3-Clause, so copyable holds. Archived 2025-08-27, 2.1k stars, not a fork; last hello_fft commit 2022-06-16 confirmed.

tier_reason: teaser-fleet-20260928.md and its JSON give single-thread FFTW (FFTW_PATIENT) inverse-only times next to matchedfilter full, peak-only and hierarchical times on seven named CPUs; all record numbers match. The harness (tools/teaser_fleet.py, tools/teaser_figure.py) and build flags (setup.py: -O3 -fno-math-errno -std=c++17) are public, but the compiler used for matchedfilter is not recorded and the two sides do unequal work (fused product + inverse FFT + peak scan vs a bare inverse FFT), so it stays first-party tier C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Milliseconds per batch (16 x 512 x 4096-point complex64, one thread), FFTW inverse-only vs matchedfilter full / peak-only / hierarchical fd=0.01 at SNR 5.5: Ryzen 9 5950X 63.63 vs 52.23 / 34.27 / 3.95; Ryzen AI Max+ 395 69.54 vs 35.12 / 20.68 / 3.12; Ryzen 5 5500U 87.45 vs 73.70 / 49.37 / 6.11; Core i5-13500H 44.96 vs 56.24 / 35.49 / 4.69; Apple M2 252.55 vs 68.75 / 57.84 / 6.28; Xeon Platinum 8260 (VM) 219.57 vs 155.19 / 79.18 / 6.24; Xeon E5-2698 v3 (contended) 178.90 vs 303.35 / 132.75 / 14.47. Peak-only is 1.86x, 3.36x, 1.77x, 1.27x, 4.37x, 2.77x and 1.35x faster than FFTW's inverse-only time (derived from page data); full output is slower than FFTW on the i5-13500H and the Haswell node. GPU (Radeon 8060S): rocFFT inverse-only 2.58 ms vs full 1.49, peak-only 0.71, hierarchical 0.20 ms; M2 GPU: MLX FFT-only 11.73 vs peak-only 3.92 ms.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: matchedfilter: setup.py builds with -O3 -fno-math-errno -std=c++17 (plus -msse4.2 -maes -mpclmul on x86) and Highway runtime dispatch (AVX2/AVX3 on the x86 hosts, NEON_BF16 on M2); compiler not recorded. FFTW baseline: pyFFTW-bundled FFTW 3.3.5 'sse2-avx' build (gcc -O2 with Fedora RPM hardening flags) on the x86 hosts, FFTW 3.3.10-neon through FFTW's C API on the M2; FFTW_PATIENT, 15 s planning limit, one thread.
corrections.caveats: First-party numbers from a young alpha repo (PyPI 0.1.0a5, 1 star). The page itself says the comparison is unequal work: FFTW and the rocFFT/MLX references time only the inverse transform, while matchedfilter also does the spectral product and peak scan and peak-only mode skips writing the output, so the gain comes from fusion and output reduction, not a faster FFT kernel; it is not a drop-in FFT. Full-output mode is slower than FFTW on the Core i5-13500H and on the Haswell node. The x86 FFTW baseline is the pyFFTW-bundled FFTW 3.3.5 built for SSE2/AVX only (no AVX2/FMA codelets), while matchedfilter dispatches to AVX2/AVX3. The M2 FFTW baseline (252.55 ms) is 3-6x slower than the x86 hosts' FFTW (44.96-87.45 ms), so the 4.37x M2 ratio likely reflects a weak arm64 FFTW build (derived from page data). The page flags the Haswell node as contended (full and hierarchical rows indicative only) and the Xeon 8260 VM as least stable. Hierarchical mode trades a false-dismissal budget for speed and these timings do not measure FDR. Compiler for matchedfilter not recorded; build flags taken from current setup.py, which may differ from revision eecb43c. Interactive pages at ahnitz.github.io were not opened (egress-blocked); repo was renamed from peak-fft and its docs mention agent handoffs, so treat claims as unreviewed.

notes: Numbers verified on the md page and in the recorded JSON (FFTW version, build and compiler per host are recorded there, contrary to the original caveat). MIT license, not a fork, last commit 2026-09-30 confirmed. Category fft is the closest wave-8 fit, but it is a fused matched filter / batched correlation, not a general FFT library.
